title: Analyse external factors influencing people who have special needs

lessons.title: Understanding physical and intellectual disabilities and their causes
lessons.html:
A wide spectrum of disability

Disability is not one condition. It is a long-term physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairment which, together with barriers in the environment and attitudes of others, limits a person's full participation in work and society. This social view of disability recognises that a ramp, a sign-language interpreter or flexible duties can remove much of the limitation.

Main categories

CategoryExamples
PhysicalAmputation, spinal injury, cerebral palsy, effects of polio, arthritis
SensoryBlindness or low vision, deafness or hearing loss
IntellectualDown syndrome, foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, other developmental intellectual disabilities
Psychosocial (mental health)Depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia when long-term and limiting
Neurological and chronicEpilepsy, effects of stroke, some chronic illnesses

Some disabilities are visible, but many, such as epilepsy, hearing loss or psychosocial disability, are hidden.

Causes

  • Before or at birth: genetic conditions, infections during pregnancy, alcohol use in pregnancy (South Africa has high rates of foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, especially in some farming regions with a history of the dop system), birth complications.
  • Disease: meningitis, TB, HIV-related conditions, diabetes leading to amputation or blindness, polio where vaccination was missed.
  • Injury: road accidents, farm machinery accidents (PTO shafts, tractor rollovers), falls, violence.
  • Ageing: hearing, vision and mobility loss.

Social and economic factors

Poverty and disability feed each other. Poor nutrition, limited access to clinics and rehabilitation, unsafe working conditions and long distances to services in rural areas raise the risk of disability, while disability makes it harder to find work and so deepens poverty. Many people with disabilities in rural areas depend on a disability grant, and families may hide a disabled member because of stigma. In agriculture, preventing injuries through safe machinery practice under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 also prevents disability.

lessons.title: Philosophy behind South African policy and legislation
lessons.html:
From charity to rights

In the past, people with disabilities were often treated as objects of charity or as patients to be cared for, separated in special institutions and excluded from mainstream work. South African policy has moved to a human rights and social model approach: people with disabilities are citizens with equal rights, and society must remove the barriers that exclude them.

Key principles

  • Equality and non-discrimination: the Constitution of 1996 lists disability as a ground on which unfair discrimination is prohibited.
  • Human dignity: treating each person with respect.
  • Inclusion and participation: people with disabilities take part in mainstream work, education and community life.
  • Reasonable accommodation: adapting the job or workplace so a qualified person can work, unless it causes unjustifiable hardship to the employer.
  • Nothing about us without us: people with disabilities are consulted on decisions that affect them.

Laws and policies

InstrumentWhat it does
Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996Equality clause includes disability
Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998Prohibits unfair discrimination; people with disabilities are a designated group for affirmative action; requires reasonable accommodation
Code of Good Practice on the employment of persons with disabilitiesGuidance to employers on recruitment, accommodation and retention
Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 4 of 2000Prohibits unfair discrimination more broadly
Skills Development Act 97 of 1998Learnerships and training that include people with disabilities
UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with DisabilitiesInternational treaty that South Africa has ratified

The national White Paper on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities sets out government's policy direction based on these principles.

Understanding this philosophy matters because it changes the question a manager asks. Instead of asking What can this person not do? the manager asks What barriers can we remove so this person can do the job?

lessons.title: Workplace practices and implications for management
lessons.html:
Reflecting on typical practices

Look honestly at how your workplace treats people with disabilities. Common practices and the values behind them include:

PracticeUnderlying value or belief
Not employing people with disabilities because the work is physicalAssumption that disability means incapacity
Giving a disabled worker only the simplest tasks regardless of skillsLow expectations, paternalism
Laying off a worker injured in a tractor accident without exploring other dutiesSeeing the person as a cost rather than an asset
Fitting a ramp and adjusting duties after asking the worker what they needRespect, inclusion, reasonable accommodation
Training supervisors in basic sign language for a deaf packhouse workerEquality and dignity

Implications for management and supervision

  • Recruitment: advertise in accessible ways, focus job requirements on what is really essential, and judge applicants on ability.
  • Reasonable accommodation: ask the person what they need. Examples on farms: a sorting table at seated height in the packshed, visual alarms for deaf workers, hand controls on a vehicle, flexible hours for medical treatment, written instructions with pictures for workers with intellectual disability.
  • Health and safety: include people with disabilities in emergency evacuation plans, for example a buddy system for a wheelchair user.
  • Return to work: after an injury, plan a phased return or alternative duties rather than automatic dismissal.
  • Confidentiality: medical information is private; share only what colleagues need to know, with consent.
  • Attitudes: challenge jokes and stereotypes; brief the team respectfully and use person-first, respectful language.
  • Development: give equal access to training and promotion.
  • Reporting: designated employers report on disability in employment equity reports.

In extension work, the same principles apply to clients: hold farmer days at accessible venues, present information verbally and visually, and include farmers with disabilities in projects.

Key points

  • Disability includes physical, sensory, intellectual, psychosocial and neurological impairments, many of them hidden.
  • Poverty, disease, injury and poor access to services contribute to disability in South Africa.
  • Policy follows a human rights and social model: remove barriers, do not exclude.
  • The Employment Equity Act requires non-discrimination and reasonable accommodation.
  • Managers should ask the person what they need, keep medical information confidential and include them in safety plans.

quiz.question: What does the social view of disability emphasise?

options.text: Disability is only a medical problem
Barriers in the environment and attitudes add to the limitation and can be removed
People with disabilities should work in separate institutions

quiz.question: Which of these is a hidden disability?

options.text: Paying a person with a disability less
Adapting the job or workplace so a qualified person can work, unless it causes unjustifiable hardship

quiz.question: Which law makes people with disabilities a designated group and requires reasonable accommodation?
A worker returns after a tractor accident. What is good management practice?

options.text: Plan a phased return or alternative duties together with the worker
Tell the whole team about the worker's medical details

A worker's medical information may be shared freely with all colleagues.

Refusing to hire anyone with a disability
